ety.text: From Early Modern English dadd, dadde (circa 1500), undoubtedly older, from unrecorded Middle English *dadde, of uncertain ultimate origin. Compare West Frisian deite (“dad, daddy”), Swabian Dede (“Godfather”). * Perhaps of Celtic origin, compare Welsh and Breton tad (from Proto-Brythonic *tad), Old Irish data; and possibly related to Russian дя́дя (djádja, “uncle”) and/or Russian де́душка (déduška, “grandfather”), all imitative. In Welsh, when subject to soft mutation (which occurs in vocative contexts, among others), tad becomes dad.
From dade (“to strike heavily”), dade (“a heavy blow or thud”). Probably onomatopoeic.

senses.d: A father, a male parent.
ex: His dad was always there for him.

senses.d: Used to address one's father; often capitalized.
Used to address an older adult male.
To be a father to; to parent.
To act like a dad.
A lump or piece.
A blow; act of striking something.
To throw against something; to dash.

grp.label: familiar address of one's own father

ety.text: French papabor. Portuguese papá Borrowed from French papa.

From Old Galician-Portuguese pay < *pade, child-speech forms of padre, from Latin patrem, the accusative of pater (“father”), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr (“father”). Doublet of padre. Compare mãe (“mother”), which underwent a similar phonetic reduction from its root (Latin mater), and, in addition, was nasalized,…
The noun is probably derived from dad (although this word is attested later) + -y (diminutive suffix). The verb is derived from the noun.
From dad + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘having the quality of’).

senses.d: Also used as a term of address: a father; one's father.
ex: By saynt Mary, my lady, / Your mammy and your dady / Brought forth a godely babi!
But unto letters vvas I alvvays ſquinting, / So aſk’d my daddy’s leave to ſtudy Printing; […]

senses.d: Often in the form the daddy of: the most important or influential man in a field or group; a doyen.
Chiefly used as a term of address: a man who is not one's father, often but not necessarily older than oneself.
ex: Rock ’n’ roll is cool, daddy, and you know it!

senses.d: Often used as a term of address: a dominant male sexual partner.
ex: The guy I’ve been dating offered to do bondage with me, and I was like “Yes please, daddy.”

senses.d: An older masculine sexual partner, especially one who is more sexually dominant; specifically, one who prefers younger partners.
A dominant partner in a homosexual relationship; especially one who provides protection to a more vulnerable inmate.
A husband; also, a woman's (often older) male lover; (generally) a sexually attractive man; a hunk.
Often in the form the daddy of: the most significant of a number of things; a perfect example.
A male juvenile delinquent in a reformatory, or a male prisoner in a prison, who dominates other inmates through threats and violence.
A man who gives away the bride at a wedding, in the absence of her actual father.
To father (a child); to beget, to sire.
Characteristic of or resembling a dad or father.
ex: […] Daddy looked at himself more these days, as if to catch himself fading away—though in Junior's eyes he was only growing Daddier.
He's the daddiest dad I've ever had.
